beats.say: Nine students each say how they get to school: walk, bus, or car.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: One dot is one student. Four students walk. Count the dots: one, two, three, four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Three students ride the bus: one, two, three.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Two come by car: one, two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: How many students is that in all? Add the three piles.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Four plus three plus two is nine. Each student is in one pile, so no one is counted twice or left out.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: So the piles always add up to the number of students. Keep that as a check.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now each student answers with a number: how many pets does the student have? Six students answered.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: How many pets does each student have?

beats.say: The answers are two, one, two, zero, two, one.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Numbers have an order, so numbers can name piles too. Here is a number line: marks in order, evenly spaced, each with its number.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Each dot drops above its student's number. The first answer is two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: One. Two again: it lands on top of the first two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The next answer is zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Zero pets means nothing. Does that student get a dot?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: A dot is one student, not one pet. This student has no pets, but is still one student. So one dot goes above zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Two again, and one again.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: This is a dot plot: one dot for each student, standing above that student's number.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Count the dots above each number. Above zero, one. Above one, two. Above two, three.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: That count is the frequency of the number: how many times the number appears in the list.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.meaning: How many times a number appears in the list. Here the number two appears three times, so its frequency is three.

beats.say: The number itself, zero, one or two, is called the value.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: A frequency table writes the same thing in numerals. The top row lists the values: zero, one, two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The bottom row gives each value's frequency: one, two, three.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: So every column has two numbers. The top one tells which pile, and the bottom one tells how many are in it.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Yes. Add the frequencies: one plus two plus three is six. That is the same six students.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: A team scored goals in each of eleven games. The list shows the goals in each game. How many games have exactly five goals?
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: These are data about the goals a team scored in each game, for 11 games: 1, 6, 0, 6, 5, 5, 6, 3, 4, 5, 5. How many games have exactly 5 goals?

beats.say: One dot is one game, so eleven dots. Drop each dot above its number, going through the list once: one, six, zero, six, five, five, six, three, four, five, five.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Exactly five means the number five and no other number.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Four dots above five. Four games, five goals each. Five, ten, fifteen, twenty. Twenty.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Test twenty. Light the stack above five and count games, not goals: one, two, three, four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Four dots are four games. Five, ten, fifteen, twenty is how many goals those games scored in all. The question asks how many games.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Check twenty against the picture. There are only eleven dots in all, so twenty games cannot be.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Then why not seven? Five or more goals is four dots at five and three dots at six.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Seven counts the stack above six as well. That stack is the games with six goals: three games, a different value.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Exactly five is only the stack above five: four games.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: A frequency is a count of dots. It is never the values added up.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Count the dots above the value. Do not add the values.

beats.say: Here is a new set of games. The dot plot shows the goals a team scored in each of eleven games. Which frequency table matches it?
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: The dot plot shows the goals a team scored in each game, for 11 games. Which frequency table matches it? The frequency of a value is how many times it appears. Each choice is written as value: frequency.

beats.say: Each choice is written value, colon, frequency. Look at five colon three: the value five has frequency three, so three dots stand above five.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Build the table first. Make a column for every number on the line, from zero to six.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: I would only make columns where dots stand: zero, one, three, five and six. Two and four have nothing above them.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Test it. Light the line at two and count the dots above it.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: None. Zero games scored two goals, and zero is a count. So two still gets a column, with frequency zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: A column for every number on the line.

beats.say: Four is the same: nothing above it, frequency zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now count from the left. Zero has two dots: frequency two. One has one dot. Two has none.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Frequency: the dots above a number.

beats.say: Three has two. Four has none. Five has three. Six has three.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Add the frequencies: two, one, zero, two, zero, three, three. That makes eleven, the number of games.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now the choices. The frequencies must add to eleven, so check each total first.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The second choice adds to ten, one short. The third adds to twelve, one too many. Neither can match eleven games.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Second choice: adds to 10. One short.
Third choice: adds to 12. One too many.

beats.say: The first and the fourth both add to eleven. Do they both match?
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: First and fourth: both add to 11.

beats.say: A total cannot catch a swap. These two differ only at zero and one. Count the dots above zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Two dots, so zero has frequency two. The first choice says one. The fourth says two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The fourth choice matches the table.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now the numbers are grouped. These are the minutes thirteen students spent on homework. Which table groups them into intervals?
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: These are data about the minutes each student spent on homework, for 13 students: 10, 3, 2, 5, 10, 4, 3, 7, 4, 0, 6, 8, 5. Which frequency table groups them into intervals? Each interval includes both of its end values. The frequency of a value is how many times it appears. Each choice is written as value: frequency.

beats.say: First, the dot plot again. Drop one dot for each student above its number: ten, three, two, five, ten, four, three, seven, four, zero, six, eight, five.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: An interval is a stretch of numbers, with both end numbers included.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.meaning: A stretch of numbers from one value to another, with both end values included. The interval 0–4 holds 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

beats.say: The interval zero to four holds zero, one, two, three and four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The table uses three intervals, all the same width.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Each one has a bracket under the line: zero to four, five to nine, ten to fourteen.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Counting by fives: zero to five, five to ten. So the fives go in the first group, and the tens in the second. Eight, five, zero.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Test it on the brackets. The first interval is zero to four, so it ends at four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The dots above five stand under the next bracket, five to nine. Each number belongs to exactly one interval.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now count each interval. Zero to four: zero, two, three, three, four, four. That is six dots.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Five to nine: five, five, six, seven, eight. That is five dots.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Ten to fourteen: ten, ten. That is two dots.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Six, five, two. That is thirteen, the number of students. But my eight, five, zero is thirteen too.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: A total cannot see which interval a dot is in. The brackets can. The total still catches a dot that is missed or counted twice.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now the choices. The first adds to fourteen. The second and third add to twelve. Only the fourth adds to thirteen.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The fourth choice matches: zero to four, six; five to nine, five; ten to fourteen, two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: One more problem, and this time Champ does the work. Fourteen runners each ran some laps. How many of them are in the interval zero to four?
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: These are data about the number of laps each runner finished, for 14 runners: 3, 3, 3, 13, 1, 12, 14, 4, 2, 10, 13, 7, 7, 6. Each interval includes both of its end values. How many are in the interval 0–4?

beats.say: Champ, start with the dot plot.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: One dot for each runner, above its number: three, three, three, thirteen, one, twelve, fourteen, four, two, ten, thirteen, seven, seven, six.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Now the interval zero to four. Which numbers does it hold?
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Zero, one, two, three and four. Both ends are in, so the dots at zero and at four count.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Count the dots inside it.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: One dot at one, one at two, three at three, one at four. That makes six.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Do the other two intervals the same way.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Five to nine holds six, seven, seven: three dots. Ten to fourteen holds ten, twelve, thirteen, thirteen, fourteen: five dots.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Now the other choices. What do fourteen, nine and three count?
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Fourteen counts every runner. Nine counts zero to four and five to nine together. Three counts only the dots above the value three.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Now answer the question that was asked.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The question asked about the interval zero to four. Six runners are in it.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Check the total.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Six plus three plus five is fourteen, the number of runners. Each runner is in exactly one interval.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Now pour the dots in each interval into one pile.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Each pile is as tall as its frequency. Draw an outline around each pile. The outline is a bar.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The bars touch, because the intervals touch. Four and five are neighbors, with no number between them.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: This picture is a histogram. Its bar heights are the numbers in the frequency table: six, three, five.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: One dot is one thing. Champ, how do you build the table?
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: First, I make a column for every number on the line, even where no dots stand.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Make a column for every number on the line, even where no dots stand.

beats.say: Next, I count the dots above each number. That count is its frequency.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Count the dots above each number: that is its frequency.

beats.say: With intervals, I count the dots under each bracket, and both end numbers are in.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: For intervals, count the dots under each bracket. Both ends are in.

beats.say: Last, I add the frequencies. The total has to be the number of dots.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Add the frequencies. The total is the number of dots.
